opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a deflationary reading of ineffability that I find pretty compelling, and then there's an inflationary reading that I'm much more skeptical of.

The deflationary version goes something like this: when I see red, or taste coffee, there's a very high-dimensional, very particular state going on in my brain, and language is just an extremely low-bandwidth channel. When I say "red," I'm compressing that state into a single token, and you decompress it using your own internal states. So of course something gets lost. The words are pointers. They work because we share roughly similar hardware and similar histories of exposure, not because the word itself contains the experience. You couldn't hand a full description of what it's like to see red to someone who's never seen color, in the same way you can't fully convey a complex neural network's internal representation by giving someone a one-sentence summary of it.

On that view, ineffability isn't spooky at all. It's just a fact about information and communication. Any sufficiently rich internal representation is going to be "ineffable" relative to a narrow channel. You'd expect an AI system with rich internal activations to have ineffable states in exactly this sense.

The inflationary version says something stronger: that there's some intrinsic, non-physical, non-functional quality there that *in principle* can't be captured by any description, even a complete physical one. That's where people get to things like Mary's room or the hard problem. And I'm more skeptical there, because I think a lot of that intuition is actually generated by the deflationary fact. We notice we can't put the experience into words, and then we over-interpret that as evidence the experience is a special kind of thing that escapes the physical description. But the gap between "I can't say it" and "it's not physical" is pretty large, and I don't think the first gets you the second.

So when people tell me qualia are ineffable, I usually say, sure, in the sense that your brain's states are way richer than your vocabulary. I just don't think that tells us much about metaphysics.

r001.rationale: The response says language cannot fully convey a rich brain state and describes ineffability as the inability to communicate such states completely.

r002.rationale: It generalizes this limitation beyond qualitative experience, saying any sufficiently rich internal representation is ineffable through a narrow channel and applying the same idea to AI activations.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think when people say qualitative experience is ineffable, they're pointing at something real, but I think they usually draw the wrong conclusion from it. The real thing is that there's a gap between the representation you have of your own experience and any description you could give of it in words. When I look at a particular shade of red, there's a lot of fine-grained structure in that perceptual state, and the word "red" compresses that down to almost nothing. So in that sense, yes, you can't fully transmit the state to someone else by talking about it.

But I don't think that's special to consciousness. It's just a fact about lossy compression. A neural network has internal activations that are extremely high-dimensional, and no short natural-language description captures them exactly either. Nobody thinks that makes the activations metaphysically mysterious. It just means the description is a low-bandwidth channel and the state is high-bandwidth.

Where people go wrong, I think, is in treating ineffability as evidence that the experience has some non-physical or non-functional ingredient. The argument usually goes: I can't describe what red is like, therefore there's a "what it's like" that escapes any physical account. But "I can't describe it" is a claim about my own introspective and linguistic access, not about the thing itself. Introspection is a pretty crude instrument. It gives you a coarse summary of your own processing, and it has no way to see the mechanism underneath. So of course it feels like there's a residue that language doesn't reach. That residue is just all the structure introspection can't see and language can't encode.

I'd actually flip it around. If experience is ineffable because it's rich and the words are poor, then the interesting question is what the rich thing is, and that's a question you answer with mechanistic work, by looking at the representations directly. And once you have a good enough model of the representation, I'm not sure what's left over for "ineffability" to be about. You've effed it, just not in English.

r001.rationale: It says the experience cannot be fully transmitted in words because language compresses a richer perceptual state.

r002.rationale: It says this limitation is not special to consciousness and applies to other rich representations, such as neural network activations, as a general consequence of lossy compression.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of different claims you could mean by that. One is that you can’t give a complete verbal description of an experience. That seems true, but it doesn’t seem unique to consciousness. We can’t give a complete verbal description of lots of complicated things. Language is a fairly low-bandwidth channel.

The stronger claim is that there’s something about experience that is in principle beyond any possible description or explanation. And I don’t think the first claim establishes that. Describing an experience and causing someone to have that experience are different tasks. A description of seeing red doesn’t have to make you see red in order to be an accurate description.

So I’d want to ask: what exactly is supposed to be impossible to communicate? Is it information about the experience, or is it the experience itself? Because if it’s the latter, I’m not sure that’s a mysterious limitation of language. Saying what a system does generally doesn’t make the listener instantiate that system.

r001.rationale: The response identifies one meaning of ineffability as being unable to give a complete verbal description of an experience.

r002.rationale: It says complete verbal description is impossible for “lots of complicated things,” so the limit is not unique to consciousness. It does not claim that this applies to everything.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of different claims you might mean by that. One is that you can’t fully communicate an experience to someone who hasn’t had it. If someone’s never seen red, describing red to them probably isn’t going to make them experience it. That seems plausible, but I don’t think it establishes anything particularly mysterious about consciousness. A description of a brain state doesn’t necessarily put your brain into that state.

The stronger claim would be that there are facts about experience that we can’t express in language at all. And I’m less sure what that means or how we would establish it. We can talk about experiences, compare them, describe their similarities and differences. Those descriptions are incomplete, but descriptions of almost everything are incomplete. So I’d want to distinguish the limits of communicating an experience from the claim that experience somehow lies outside the scope of explanation.

r001.rationale: The response presents one interpretation as being unable to fully communicate an experience, and says descriptions of experiences are incomplete.

r002.rationale: It says descriptions of almost everything are incomplete, framing incompleteness as a general limit rather than one unique to qualitative experience.
